```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
Introduction

This notebook demonstrates how to choose and apply common statistical tests based on:

variable types (categorical vs numeric),

number of groups,

distributional assumptions,

the research question (association vs group differences).

We use the Palmer Penguins dataset as a worked example.

Objectives

We demonstrate four common scenarios:

Two categorical variables (multi-category) → association test

Two numeric variables → correlation test

One categorical variable (3+ groups) + one numeric variable → group comparison

One categorical variable (2 groups) + one numeric variable → two-sample comparison

Setup
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(psych)
library(gmodels)
library(dunn.test)
library(palmerpenguins)

# Load data (portable)
data("penguins")
penguins_df <- penguins %>% 
  clean_names()

# Quick structure check
str(penguins_df)
Data overview (descriptive statistics)
Species distribution
penguins_df %>%
  drop_na(species) %>%
  count(species) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(species, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Penguin species counts", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
Summary by species (example: culmen length)
penguins_df %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(bill_length_mm)),
    min = min(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1 = quantile(bill_length_mm, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(bill_length_mm, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

Note: In the palmerpenguins package, culmen variables are called bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm.

Hypotheses

H1: Penguin species are associated with the island they inhabit.

H2: Bill length is associated with bill depth.

H3: Penguin species differ in flipper length.

H4: Penguin body mass differs by sex (within species).

H1 — Categorical vs Categorical (Chi-square)
Question

Are species and island associated?

Variables

species: categorical (3 levels)

island: categorical (3 levels)

Test choice

Chi-square test of independence

Check expected counts to confirm suitability

df_h1 <- penguins_df %>% drop_na(species, island)

tbl <- table(df_h1$species, df_h1$island)
tbl

chisq_res <- chisq.test(tbl)
chisq_res

# Expected counts (assumption check)
chisq_res$expected
Interpretation

If p-value < 0.05, we reject H0 (independence) and conclude species and island are associated.

H2 — Numeric vs Numeric (Correlation)
Question

Is bill length associated with bill depth?

Variables

bill_length_mm: numeric

bill_depth_mm: numeric

Assumption check (normality overview)

We use Shapiro-Wilk as a quick diagnostic (note: it is sensitive in larger samples),
and we also inspect density plots.

df_h2 <- penguins_df %>% drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)

# Quick distribution plots
ggplot(df_h2, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Density: Bill length (mm)", x = "bill_length_mm", y = "Density")

ggplot(df_h2, aes(x = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_density() + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Density: Bill depth (mm)", x = "bill_depth_mm", y = "Density")

# Shapiro tests
shapiro.test(df_h2$bill_length_mm)
shapiro.test(df_h2$bill_depth_mm)
Test choice

If normality is questionable, use Spearman (rank correlation).
We also show Kendall as a robustness check.

spearman_res <- cor.test(df_h2$bill_length_mm, df_h2$bill_depth_mm, method = "spearman")
spearman_res

kendall_res <- cor.test(df_h2$bill_length_mm, df_h2$bill_depth_mm, method = "kendall")
kendall_res
Interpretation

Report:

correlation coefficient (rho or tau),

p-value,

direction and strength.

H3 — Categorical (3+ groups) vs Numeric (Kruskal–Wallis + Dunn)
Question

Do species differ in flipper length?

Variables

species: categorical (3 levels)

flipper_length_mm: numeric

Assumption check (normality within groups)
df_h3 <- penguins_df %>% drop_na(species, flipper_length_mm)

df_h3 %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(flipper_length_mm)$p.value, n = n())
Test choice

If at least one group deviates from normality, use Kruskal–Wallis.
If significant, follow with Dunn post-hoc (Bonferroni).

kw_res <- kruskal.test(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = df_h3)
kw_res

# Post-hoc (pairwise comparisons)
dunn_res <- dunn.test(df_h3$flipper_length_mm, df_h3$species, method = "bonferroni")
dunn_res
Interpretation

Kruskal–Wallis tests whether at least one group differs.

Dunn indicates which pairs differ after correction.

H4 — Categorical (2 groups) vs Numeric (t-test within species)
Question

Does sex relate to body mass, within each species?

Variables

sex: categorical (male/female)

body_mass_g: numeric

Data cleaning
df_h4 <- penguins_df %>%
  filter(sex %in% c("male", "female")) %>%
  drop_na(species, sex, body_mass_g)

table(df_h4$sex)
Assumption check (normality within sex groups, per species)
df_h4 %>%
  group_by(species, sex) %>%
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(body_mass_g)$p.value, n = n())
Test choice + implementation

Independent two-sample t-test per species (as in your notebook).

t_results <- df_h4 %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    p_value = t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex)$p.value,
    mean_male = mean(body_mass_g[sex == "male"]),
    mean_female = mean(body_mass_g[sex == "female"]),
    n_male = sum(sex == "male"),
    n_female = sum(sex == "female")
  )

t_results
Interpretation

If p-value < 0.05, reject H0 and conclude body mass differs by sex (within species).

Summary (What this notebook demonstrates)
summary_table <- tibble(
  hypothesis = c(
    "H1: species ~ island",
    "H2: bill_length ~ bill_depth",
    "H3: flipper_length ~ species",
    "H4: body_mass ~ sex (within species)"
  ),
  variable_types = c(
    "categorical vs categorical",
    "numeric vs numeric",
    "categorical (3+) vs numeric",
    "categorical (2) vs numeric"
  ),
  chosen_test = c(
    "Chi-square",
    "Spearman (+ Kendall)",
    "Kruskal–Wallis + Dunn post-hoc",
    "t-test per species"
  )
)

summary_table
Notes

Claims about normality should not rely on a single test alone; visual inspection helps.

For group comparisons, always consider effect sizes and confidence intervals when relevant.

This notebook focuses on test selection logic and clear reporting, rather than maximizing model complexity.

References

Palmer Penguins dataset (R package: palmerpenguins)
